title: SRE documentation standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident reviews, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Purpose
This document defines Redwood Inference SRE documentation standards covering SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and runbook structure. The goal is consistent, actionable, and auditable SRE docs that make oncall responses predictable, enable capacity decisions, and support cross-team reliability work.

Scope
Applies to all production-facing services (hosted API, dedicated control plane, private deployment control plane) and platform components (routing, cache, GPU pool allocator). This is a standards doc: individual services provide SLOs, runbooks, and capacity plans that follow these templates.

1) High-level requirements for SLO docs
- Each service must publish an SLO page containing the following explicit fields: service name, owner(s), SLI definitions, SLO target(s), measurement window, data sources, error budget policy, and alerting thresholds.
- SLO naming convention: <service>-<intent>-<metric>-<window>. Example: api-latency-p95-30d.
- Minimum SLOs required for customer-facing services: availability (request success rate), latency (P95 for interactive endpoints), and correctness where applicable (model output correctness / QA metric).
- SLO targets guidance (suggested defaults):
  - Customer-facing API availability: 99.9% monthly (SLO name: api-availability-99.9-30d)
  - Interactive generation latency: P95 <= 500ms for small models / <= 1s for larger family variants (adjust per model family)
  - Embeddings: P95 <= 200ms
  - Batch inference throughput SLOs: configured by contract (e.g., guaranteed 1000 requests/hour)
- Measurement window: default 30d rolling; teams may add 7d and 90d views for operational perspective.

SLI & instrumentation standards
- All SLIs must be derived from reliable, instrumented signals (ingress request logs, LB metrics, internal RPC traces). Do not use synthetic or debug-only signals as primary SLI without justification.
- Recording rules: store raw counters and aggregated time-series used to compute SLIs in our central metrics cluster (prometheus -> Cortex). Provide the exact grafana expression / prometheus query on the SLO page.
- Example SLI definitions (text + query snippet):
  - api-success-rate: fraction of requests with status in [200, 201, 202] over total requests. Query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",code=~"2.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m]))
  - api-latency-p95: 95th percentile of request duration measured at ingress. Query: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[5m])) by (le))

2) Error budget policy and burn management
- Default error budget window: 30d rolling. Error budget = (1 - SLO_target) * 30d (expressed appropriately for rate or latency objectives).
- Burn rate thresholds and automated actions (minimum required):
  1) Normal: burn_rate <= 1. No action.
  2) Elevated: burn_rate > 1 and <= 4 -> notify owner + oncall, start triage.
  3) Critical: burn_rate > 4 -> page senior oncall, halt non-essential launches/rollouts, and open high-priority incident.
- Error budget playbook (ordered steps):
  1. Verify SLI data source correctness (last 15 min)
  2. Triage root cause (incidents, capacity, config, model degradation)
  3. If outage / persistent burn, trigger rollback or fallback policy (e.g., route to lower-latency model variant or reduce max tokens)
  4. If burn persists, initiate release freeze for affected components and notify product/PMs
  5. Document actions in the SLO page and link to incident review
- Enforcement: Platform and governance teams will check error budgets in monthly reliability reviews. Persistent deficits require a reliability initiative defined below.

3) Capacity planning documentation standards
- Every service must publish an annual capacity plan and a rolling 90-day operational capacity forecast. Plans must include:
  - Baseline metrics: current 95th/99th utilization for compute, GPU pool consumption, network egress, IOPS where relevant
  - Forecast assumptions: growth rate (traffic, customers), model mix changes, seasonality, and key upcoming launches
  - Safety buffer policy: maintain minimum 20% spare capacity for customer-facing clusters and 30% for Dedicated pools in the first six months after launch
  - Scaling policies: autoscaling thresholds, cooldowns, and manual scale playbook with required approvals
  - Cost vs reliability trade-offs: recommended quantization/packing features and their quality impact (link to quantization profiles page)

Capacity forecasting checklist (required fields on capacity plan page):
1. Time-series for last 12 months (QPS, requests/hour, vGPU-hours)
2. Peak day analysis (present at least 3 historical peaks)
3. Headroom calculations and safety buffer rationale
4. Runbook for emergency capacity increases (manual scale steps and expected lead time)

4) Reliability initiatives and project docs
- When a service experiences repeated error budget exhaustion or misses major SLOs for > 2 consecutive months, a Reliability Initiative (RI) is required. RI doc must include: owner, goal/target, baseline metrics, proposed workstreams, success criteria (measurable), timeline, and tracked blockers.
- Typical RI workstreams: caching improvements, batching/packing, kernel-level optimizations, routing policy changes, circuit breakers, and increased observability (new SLIs).
- Tracking: RIs are tracked in the reliability backlog board and receive monthly review in the SRE leadership meeting.

5) Incident review & postmortem standards
- Every incident meeting the severity threshold (pages) must produce a written postmortem within 72h. Postmortem structure (required sections):
  - Summary: one-paragraph incident overview (what, impact, duration)
  - Timeline: minute-level key events (edit with timestamps)
  - Root cause analysis: factual causal chain (avoid finger-pointing)
  - Impact metrics: users affected, error budget consumed, cost impact estimate
  - Remediation & mitigating actions taken during incident
  - Long-term follow-up tasks & owners (link to Reliability Initiative if needed)
  - Lessons learned and preventive actions (concrete design/operational changes)
- Severity classification guidance: Sev2 = degraded but partial functionality; Sev1 = customer-visible outage affecting multiple customers or SLAs. Postmortems for Sev1 require an executive summary and presentation to leadership.

6) Operational tooling & dashboards
- Standard dashboards (every service must have):
  - SLO dashboard: current SLI vs SLO, error budget remaining, burn rate, 7/30/90d views
  - Health dashboard: request rate, P50/P95/P99 latency, success rate, CPU/GPU utilization, queue lengths
  - Incident triage dashboard: recent errors, top traces, slow queries
- Alerting standards:
  - Use a two-tier alert model: Page for Sev1-level signals (hard SLO breaches or critical capacity) and non-paging alerts for degraded but actionable conditions (Slack + ticket)
  - Avoid noisy low-fidelity alerts: every alert must include runbook link, required context, and suggested remediation steps
- Tooling integrations: link SLO pages to grafana panels, oncall rota, Runbook DB, and incident tracker (PagerDuty/Jira). Provide exact dashboard IDs on the SLO page.

7) Runbook standards and templates
- Runbook format (required fields):
  - Title
  - Service and component
  - Owner and escalation chain (names + Pduty roles)
  - Symptoms (what you’ll observe)
  - Immediate triage steps (numbered)
  - Safe rollback/fallback commands (copy-paste CLI snippets)
  - Mitigations to reduce impact (e.g., reduce concurrency, adjust routing)
  - Post-incident actions and links to relevant dashboards/logs
- Example runbook excerpt for API latency spike:
  1) Check SLO dashboard: confirm P95 > target and check burn rate
  2) Inspect ingress error logs: top error codes and trace IDs
  3) Check GPU pool allocator: vGPU utilization and queue length
  4) If backend queue > 5000 items, scale up worker pool (CLI):
     - kubectl scale deployment api-workers --replicas=12 --namespace=prod
  5) If model variance is causing slowness, route 20% traffic to smaller model:
     - curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' https://controlplane/redwood/routing -d '{"route":"/generate","variant":"fast-1","weight":20}'

8) Documentation hygiene and review cadence
- SLO pages, capacity plans, and runbooks must be reviewed quarterly by service owners and SRE representatives. Reviews are recorded with a short changelog entry on the page.
- Ownership handover: when owners change, the outgoing owner must perform a documentation handover and update the page owner field.
- Quality gate: any new service onboarding requires SRE signoff on SLO definitions and runbooks before production traffic is allowed.

Appendices
A. SLO checklist (copy into new SLO pages)
- SLI queries (exact)
- SLO target & rationale
- Measurement window
- Error budget policy (notifications + actions)
- Dashboards (IDs)
- Runbook link

B. Incident severity rubric (quick reference)
- Sev1: >10% customers affected OR complete region outage OR data loss. Page + exec report.
- Sev2: single-customer large impact OR multi-customer degraded performance. Page + postmortem.
- Sev3: minor impact, no paging. Document in incident tracker.
